title: Categorical homotopy equivalences of Segal spaces preserve mapping spaces
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes, homotopy fibers and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and the Reedy model structure of [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. A simplicial space is a functor $V:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$. It is a Segal space if it is Reedy fibrant and its consecutive-edge maps $V_n\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ are weak homotopy equivalences for every $n\geq2$. For vertices $x,y$ of $V_0$, let $M_V(x,y)$ be the strict fiber of $(d_1,d_0):V_1\to V_0^2$. The homotopy category $hV$ has those vertices as objects, morphisms $\pi_0M_V(x,y)$, identity from $s_0$, and composition from the degree-two Segal map and $d_1$. Let $V_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq V_1$ be the union of components representing isomorphisms in $hV$.

For $n\geq0$ let $F(n)_k=\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([k],[n])$, discrete in the inner direction. Let $I[1]$ be the groupoid on objects $0,1$ with exactly one morphism between each ordered pair, and let $E$ be its ordinary nerve, regarded as a simplicial space discrete in the inner direction. Let $e_0,e_1:F(0)\to E$ select the two objects, and let $a:F(1)\to E$ select the arrow $0\to1$. For maps $f_0,f_1:A\to B$ of simplicial spaces, a categorical homotopy means a map $H:A\times E\to B$ restricting to $f_0,f_1$ at $e_0,e_1$. Let $U,V$ be Segal spaces and let $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to U$ be maps. If $gf$ and $1_U$ are categorically homotopic and $fg$ and $1_V$ are categorically homotopic, then
$$M_U(x,y)\longrightarrow M_V(fx,fy)$$
is a weak homotopy equivalence for all vertices $x,y\in U_0$, and $hf:hU\to hV$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories. In particular every object of $hV$ is isomorphic to some $f(x)$.

source.place: Sections 13.1, 13.3 and Proposition 13.8, using Lemma 13.9; printed pp. 29-32. The stated common-inverse version is a special case of the two-inverse formulation there. Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Use the term Dwyer--Kan equivalence with the two conditions spelled out in [lem-coef-segal-cotensor-evaluation-dk]. By [lem-coef-segal-cartesian-exponent], $U^E$ and $V^E$ are Segal spaces with the displayed cartesian internal hom. Denote their endpoint evaluations by $p_i^U:U^E\to U$ and $p_i^V:V^E\to V$. Both endpoint maps for each space are Dwyer--Kan equivalences by [lem-coef-segal-cotensor-evaluation-dk]. Choose the given homotopies with restrictions $(gf,1_U)$ and $(fg,1_V)$ at $(e_0,e_1)$, interchanging $0$ and $1$ in $E$ if needed. Curry them to maps $k_U:U\to U^E$ and $k_V:V\to V^E$. Explicitly, $cK$ denotes the constant simplicial space on a simplicial set $K$. On an $(n,q)$-simplex $u:F(n)\times c\Delta^q\to U$, $k_U(u)$ is the composite $E\times F(n)\times c\Delta^q\xrightarrow{(u\circ\operatorname{pr}_{F(n)\times c\Delta^q},\operatorname{pr}_E)}U\times E\xrightarrow{H_U}U$. On an $(n,q)$-simplex $v:F(n)\times c\Delta^q\to V$, $k_V(v)$ is the composite $E\times F(n)\times c\Delta^q\xrightarrow{(v\circ\operatorname{pr}_{F(n)\times c\Delta^q},\operatorname{pr}_E)}V\times E\xrightarrow{H_V}V$. Precomposition commutes with these formulas, so these are maps of simplicial spaces. Restriction at $e_i$ gives the strict identities $p_0^Uk_U=gf$, $p_1^Uk_U=1_U$, $p_0^Vk_V=fg$, $p_1^Vk_V=1_V$.

source.place: Sections 2.3 and 13.1; Lemma 13.9, used in the two diagrams of the proof of Proposition 13.8, printed pp. 29-31.

proof.text: Apply the two-out-of-six clause of [lem-coef-segal-dk-two-out-of-six] to the composable triple $U\xrightarrow{k_U}U^E\xrightarrow{p_1^U}U\xrightarrow{1_U}U$. Its adjacent composites are $1_U$ and $p_1^U$, respectively. The identity is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence directly from the definition: its induced maps on every mapping space and on the homotopy category are identities. The map $p_1^U$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence by step 1. Thus $k_U$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Since $p_0^U$ is one as well, the composition clause of the same cited node makes $gf=p_0^Uk_U$ a Dwyer--Kan equivalence.

source.place: Proposition 13.8, first diagram, using Lemmas 13.9 and 7.5; the cancellation is written as the explicit triple (k_U,p_1^U,1_U).

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-segal-dk-two-out-of-six] to $V\xrightarrow{k_V}V^E\xrightarrow{p_1^V}V\xrightarrow{1_V}V$. The adjacent composites are $1_V$ and $p_1^V$; the first has identity maps on all mapping spaces and on $hV$, and the second is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence by step 1. Hence $k_V$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Composing it with $p_0^V$, using the composition clause of the cited node, gives that $fg=p_0^Vk_V$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence.

source.place: Proposition 13.8, second diagram, using Lemmas 13.9 and 7.5; the cancellation is written as the explicit triple (k_V,p_1^V,1_V).

proof.text: Finally apply the two-out-of-six clause of [lem-coef-segal-dk-two-out-of-six] to $U\xrightarrow{f}V\xrightarrow{g}U\xrightarrow{f}V$. Its adjacent composites $gf$ and $fg$ are Dwyer--Kan equivalences by steps 2 and 3, so $f$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. By the definition in the cited statement this gives both the weak homotopy equivalence $M_U(x,y)\to M_V(fx,fy)$ for every pair of vertices and the equivalence $hf:hU\to hV$. In particular essential surjectivity of that equivalence means that every object of $hV$ is isomorphic to some $f(x)$, exactly the last assertion.

source.place: Last sentence of the proof of Proposition 13.8, printed p. 31, using Lemma 7.5 and the definition in Section 7.4.

proof_origin.place: Explicit currying and two-out-of-six reconstruction of Proposition 13.8 from Lemmas 13.9 and 7.5. Read online, but archive absent; WANTED recorded in report.md.
